theme: Healing at Bethesda; the Son’s authority; witnesses to Jesus
readingInstruction: Read John 5:1-47. Jesus heals a man at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath, and the leaders want to kill him. He then speaks at length about his relationship to the Father. Notice the claims he makes.
settingTheScene: Jesus returns to Jerusalem for a feast. At the pool of Bethesda, many sick people lie waiting for healing. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus heals him, and since it is the Sabbath, the leaders object. What follows is one of the longest and most direct claims to deity in the Gospels. Jesus makes himself equal to the Father in work, honor, and authority, and then lists the witnesses to his claim.
observation: “Get up, take up your bed, and walk” (5:8).
“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (5:17).
“Calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (5:18).
“Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (5:24).
“The hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (5:25).
“You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me” (5:39).
“For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (5:46).
interpretation:
The man by the pool is helpless. He has no one to put him in the water. Jesus asks, “Do you want to be healed?” and instead of answering yes, the man gives an excuse. Jesus does not need his help. He says, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk,” and the man is healed at once. The man did nothing to earn it. This is grace.

The leaders do not rejoice. The healing was on the Sabbath, and the man is carrying his mat. When they persecute Jesus, he answers, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” God does not stop working on the Sabbath, because he sustains the world and upholds the lives of his creatures. Jesus claims the same prerogative. The leaders understand perfectly: he is “making himself equal with God,” and they seek to kill him.

Jesus does not retreat. He doubles down. The Son does only what he sees the Father doing. The Father shows him everything. Like the Father, he raises the dead and gives life to whom he will. The Father has given all judgment to the Son, “that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father.” Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father. And then, a promise: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.” Eternal life is not only future. Believers have already passed from death to life.

Jesus then lists witnesses: John the Baptist, the works he does, the Father himself, and the Scriptures. The leaders search the Scriptures, thinking they give life, but they refuse to come to him. The Scriptures are not an end in themselves. They point to him. “Moses wrote of me.” It is possible to study the Bible diligently and still miss its center. The leaders are an example of how not to read, and Jesus teaches us to read the Scriptures to find Christ.
connection: Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:12-15 give the Sabbath commandment. Isaiah 40:28 says God does not grow weary. Daniel 7:13-14 gives the Son of Man authority. Daniel 12:2 speaks of the resurrection of the dead. Deuteronomy 18:15-19 promises a prophet like Moses. Luke 24:27 and 24:44 say the Scriptures speak of Christ. Romans 5:1 and 8:1 say there is now no condemnation. Ephesians 2:4-5 says we are made alive.
application:
Answer Jesus’ question honestly: do you want to be healed? Where do you make excuses?

When you read the Bible, ask: where does this point to Jesus?

Thank God that you have passed from death to life. Say it aloud.
prayerPrompts: Tell Jesus you are helpless, and let him ask whether you want to be healed.
Thank him that he heals by his word alone.
Ask him to give you life.
